title: The Minimum Formula Size Problem is (ETH) Hard
abstract: A longstanding open question is whether the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP) is NP-complete. In fact, even determining whether MCSP has a search-to-decision reduction has been open for over twenty years. We show that, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, the Minimum (DeMorgan) Formula Size Problem, MFSP, is not in P. Building on this, we show that MFSP has a polynomial-time (exact) search-to-decision reduction, a result that does not relativize. Our main technique relates the formula complexity of a partial function with the formula complexity of an associated total function and is proved using the "leaf weighting'' technique of Buchfuhrer and Umans.

Ideally, one would be able to prove MCSP is NPcomplete. Besides characterizing the complexity of a natural
optimization problem, this would also extend many of the
intriguing properties known for MCSP to NP. For example,
Hirahara [10] shows that if a certain approximation to MCSP
is NP-complete, then NP has a worst-case to averagecase reduction, resolving a longstanding open question in
average-case complexity.
Despite this signiﬁcant motivation, a proof that MCSP is
NP-complete (or, conversely, evidence that it is unlikely to
be NP-complete) remains elusive. Researchers have, however, discovered signiﬁcant technical barriers to showing
that MCSP is NP-hard [3], [8], [14]–[16]. These technical
barriers do not suggest that MCSP is or is not likely
NP-hard, they just imply that proving NP-hardness would
be difﬁcult. For example, Murray and Williams [3] show
that if MCSP is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one
reductions, then EXP = ZPP. Note that EXP = ZPP is
a consequence we believe but seems difﬁcult to show. At
heart, these technical barriers boil down to the following
intuition5 : any proof of hardness for MCSP implicitly shows
how to “efﬁciently generate” intractable NO instances for
MCSP, but intractable NO instances of MCSP correspond
to functions that require large circuits, and we do not know
how to produce explicit hard functions.
This raises a natural question: is the difﬁculty of showing
that MCSP is, say, NP-complete primarily because of a
lack of techniques (in particular, a lack of circuit lower
bounds) or is it because it is actually just false? Could
it be that MCSP is a hard problem, but just not an NPhard problem? In support of the latter possibility, Allender
and Hirahara [17] show that, for very large approximation
factors, approximating MCSP is not NP-complete under a
cryptographic assumption.

Abstract—A longstanding open question is whether the
Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP) is NP-complete. In
fact, even determining whether MCSP has a search-to-decision
reduction has been open for over twenty years.
We show that, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis,
the Minimum (DeMorgan) Formula Size Problem, MFSP,
is not in P. Building on this, we show that MFSP has a
polynomial-time (exact) search-to-decision reduction, a result
that does not relativize. Our main technique relates the formula

Keywords-Minimum Formula Size Problem, Minimum Circuit Size Problem, Boolean Formulas, Meta-Complexity

I. T HE M INIMUM C IRCUIT S IZE P ROBLEM
The1 Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP) asks one
to determine whether a given function f (represented by its
truth table) has a circuit of a given size s. While it is easy
to see that this problem is in NP2 , it is a longstanding open
question whether MCSP is NP-complete. Indeed, research
on the intractability of MCSP dates back at least to the
1950s (see Traktenbrot [1] for a historical survey), and Levin
actually delayed publishing his results on the theory of NPcompleteness, in part because he hoped to show MCSP is
NP-complete [2].
Interest in MCSP is further motivated by a growing number of intriguing connections between MCSP and areas such
as pseudorandomness [3], [4], cryptography [4], [5], learning
theory [6], circuit complexity [7], [8], proof complexity [9],
and average-case complexity [10]3 .
A. How Hard is MCSP?
The main motivation of our paper is to further understand
the hardness of MCSP and its variants. Empirically, MCSP
seems to be an intractable problem. Indeed, we do not
know any algorithm for solving MCSP better than bruteforce search. On the other hand, so far the intractability of

an intermediate task over two decades ago: Does MCSP
have a polynomial-time search-to-decision reduction? All
NP-complete problems have a search-to-decision reduction
(because SAT has one), so ﬁnding a search-to-decision
reduction is a necessary step to showing that MCSP is NPhard.
Over two decades since Kabanets and Cai raised the question, the problem is still wide open. Carmosino, Impagliazzo,
Kabanets and Kolokolova [6] proved an “approximate”
search-to-decision reduction (where instead of outputting
an optimal circuit, you output an approximately optimal
circuit that computes the function on most of its inputs), and
Hirahara [10] and Santhanam [4] prove further extensions
of this result. But it is still open to refute the possibility
that the decision version of MCSP can be solved in, say,
linear-time and the search version requires exponential-time.
Recently, Ren and Santhanam [18] gave a partial explanation
for this: there is a relativized world where the search problem
requires nearly exponential time but the decision version is
in linear-time. As a result, proving a polynomial-time searchto-decision reduction for MCSP requires non-relativizing
techniques.
Given the above discussion, one may feel somewhat
pessimistic about the possibility of proving NP-hardness
of MCSP, at least without a major breakthrough. Luckily, the aforementioned technical barriers against proving NP-hardness disappear if one relaxes the notion of
reduction from, say, polynomial-time reductions to, say,
subexponential-time reductions. In particular, we already
know functions that require linear-sized circuits (e.g. any
function that depends on all of its inputs), and the bruteforce algorithm for solving MCSP on functions with linearsized6 circuits requires superpolynomial-time. As a result,
one could hope to show that MCSP is not in P under, say,
the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) by utilizing existing
lower bound techniques. Indeed, we conjecture that this is
the case.

II. T HE M INIMUM F ORMULA S IZE P ROBLEM
Our results focus on the formula version of MCSP, the
Minimum Formula Size Problem (MFSP). Formally, MFSP
is the problem of
2n
• Given: the truth table T ∈ {0, 1}
of a function
f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} and a positive integer s
• Determine: if there is a De Morgan formula with at
most s leaves that computes f .
Our convention is to let N = 2n denote the length of the
truth table and let n denote the number of inputs to f .
We remark that we have deﬁned MFSP using the model
of De Morgan formulas (i.e. formulas with AND, OR, and
NOT gates). This is the usual notion of formulas, however,
we note that this choice will be important for our results.
We discuss this in more detail when we present our results
in Section III.
Our understanding of MFSP is in a similar state as our
understanding of MCSP. We know that neither problem can
be in P under various cryptographic assumptions, like the
intractability of factoring Blum integers [7], [8], [22]. We
also know that both MCSP and MFSP are not in AC0 [⊕]
[23]. Finally, we know that the partial function versions of
both MFSP and MCSP are not in P under ETH [19]. Note:
the discussion in [19] focuses on the partial function version
of MCSP, however, [19] notes that proof also shows that the
result in the case of formulas (in fact even in the case of
read-once formulas!). This theorem will be crucial for our
results.
There are some results, however, that are not known to
hold for both MCSP and MFSP. While Allender and Das
[12] prove MCSP is be hard for SZK, SZK-hardness is
still open for MFSP. Also, [24] shows a better than bruteforce search-to-decision reduction for MFSP (it runs in time
2.67N ), while such a reduction is not known for MCSP.
III. R ESULTS AND D ISCUSSION
Our main technical contribution is showing a relationship
between the formula complexity of an arbitrary partial
function γ and the formula complexity of a related total
function Extend[γ, s]. In order to state this more formally,
we introduce some notation. Let γ : {0, 1}n → {0, 1, } be
a partial function. Let g  : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} be the total
function that outputs 1 on input x if and only if γ(x) = .
Finally, let L(γ) denote the size of the smallest formula that
computes a total function that agrees with γ.
Our main technical lemma is as follows.

Conjecture 1. If ETH is true, then solving MCSP on
functions f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} with a size threshold
s ≤ O(n) is not in P.
Ilango [19] recently showed the above conjecture is true
for Partial-MCSP, the partial function version of MCSP,
where instead of being provided with a truth table T of

Note that Extend[γ, s] and g  are both total functions. As
a result, one could use Lemma 2 to compute the formula
complexity of a partial function γ : {0, 1}n → {0, 1, }
in time 2O(s+n) , using an oracle to MFSP, if one could
somehow correctly guess a value of s ≥ min{L(γ), L(g  )}.
We remark that the quantity min{L(γ), L(g  )} seems somewhat strange, but it arises naturally in the proof and that the
structure of this upper bound turns out to be crucial for our
results.
One of the main ideas we use to prove Lemma 2 is the
“leaf weighting” technique of Buchfuhrer and Umans [25],
who use the technique to show that the Σ2 P version of
MFSP (i.e. the problem of given a formula ϕ and a size
threshold s, determining if there exists a formula of size
at most s computing the same function as ϕ) is hard for
Σ2 P. The leaf weighting technique allows one to give a
weight k to an input variable z by replacing it with an OR
of k new inputs z1 , . . . , zk . Buchfuhrer and Umans show
that this construction effectively forces that any formula that
wants to read z to pay for k leaves instead of just one.
In our construction of Extend[γ, s], certain inputs are given
weight s and if s ≥ min{L(γ), L(g  )}, we show that those
inputs can appear at most once in any optimal formula for
Extend[γ, s]. This constrains any optimal formula enough to
prove the lemma.
We note that using the leaf weighting technique is extremely expensive, as even adding just one extra variable
(i.e. increasing the weight of a variable by one) doubles
the total size of the truth table. As a result, in order to get
efﬁcient reductions (in our case, one subexponential-time
reduction and one polynomial-time reduction) one needs to
be rather thrifty in applying leaf weighting. Indeed, it is
particularly surprising that leaf weighting is useful at all
(let alone crucially important) in our proof that there is a
polynomial-time search-to-decision reduction for MFSP.
We now discuss how we use Lemma 2 to prove our two
main results. As we mentioned previously, [19] showed that
the partial function version of MCSP is hard under ETH. As
noted in [19], the proof also shows that the partial function
version of MFSP is hard under ETH. In fact this hardness
result applies when one is promised that L(γ) ≤ 10n.

In fact the above hardness result holds even assuming
the size parameter s is restricted to be at most O(n10 ).8
In comparison, the brute force algorithm runs in time at
10
most N O(log log n) on these type of instances, so our
(conditional) lower bound is optimal up to a constant power
in the exponent. This is interesting from the perspective
of recent hardness magniﬁcation results [26]–[30], which
show that weak lower bounds against MCSP-like problems
with small size thresholds imply strong lower bounds. For
example, implicit in McKay, Murray, and Williams [29]
is the result that if MFSP with size parameter restricted
to being s ≤ O(n10 ) does not have a circuit of size
n · poly log n, then NP does not have polynomial-sized
circuits. Our result proves a partial converse. If MFSP with
size parameter restricted to being s ≤ O(n10 ) has a circuit
of size N o(log log N ) , then the non-uniform version of ETH
is false.
Our second main result is a polynomial-time search-todecision reduction for MFSP.

On the other hand, we can use Lemma 2 to compute L(γ)
in time 2O(n) = poly(N ) with an oracle to MFSP if we are

Thus, we get the following theorem.

At a high-level, our algorithm is very intuitive. It works
by combining the ideas used in the “better than bruteforce” search-to-decision reduction in [24] with Lemma 2.
In particular, given any “non-trivial” total function f :
{0, 1}n → {0, 1}, we show how, using an oracle to MFSP,
one can efﬁciently ﬁnd functions g, h : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}
such that there is an optimal formula for f where the top
two subformulas feeding into the output gate compute g and
h respectively. We call such a (g, h) pair an optimal decomposition of f . By repeatedly ﬁnding optimal decompositions,
one can recursively build an optimal formula for f .
Our method for ﬁnding an optimal decomposition (g, h)
is to construct a partial function OrSelect[f, γ, ζ] such that
if γ, ζ : {0, 1}n → {0, 1, } are partial functions satisfying a certain condition, then the formula complexity of
OrSelect[f, γ, ζ] is small if and only if there is an optimal
decomposition (g, h) such that g agrees with γ and h agrees
with ζ. Since Lemma 2 gives us a way of calculating the
formula complexity of the partial function OrSelect[f, γ, ζ]
using an oracle to MFSP, this allows us to ﬁnd g and h
by building them up bit-by-bit from γ and ζ. While this
approach is quite intuitive, it runs into a serious problem:
applying Lemma 2 to convert partial function queries into
total function queries is very expensive. In general, it uses
exponential-time. In order to implement this procedure in
polynomial-time, it is critical to take a more ﬁne-grained
approach: using the upper bound of L(g  ) on the quantity
min{L(γ), L(g  )} in the statement of Lemma 2 and carefully

Intriguingly, this result does not relativize. Santhanam and
Ren [18] show that there is an oracle relative to which MCSP
can be solved in deterministic linear time, but the search
version of MCSP requires deterministic time 2Ω(N/ log N ) .
Their proof also shows the same oracle separation for
MFSP. As a result, we can conclude that our search-todecision reduction does not relativize. This relativization
barrier means that any polynomial-time search-to-decision
reduction for MFSP must make signiﬁcant use of properties
of the underlying gate set. Our reduction does this, as our
techniques rely heavily on the underlying gate set being
AND, OR, and NOT. Indeed, it is not even clear whether
our results extend to the B2 basis consisting of all Boolean
functions from two bits to one!9

A. Further Related Work
While it is beyond the scope of this work to give an
exhaustive review of the literature on MCSP, there are
several related works that we have not yet discussed that
are worth mentioning.
One can view our hardness result for MFSP as ﬁtting
in a general line of work of showing hardness of MCSP
for restricted circuit classes. Masek [31] shows that the
DNF version of MCSP is NP-hard, and a long line of
work [20], [32]–[35] culminates in near-optimal hardness
of approximation for the DNF version. Hirahara, Oliveira,
and Santhanam [21] extend Masek’s result to show NPhardness for the version of MCSP for DNF circuits with
parity gates at the bottom. Finally, [19] shows that the
constant depth formula version of MCSP is NP-hard (under
quasipolynomial-time randomized reductions).
In the realm of general circuits, the conditional version of
MCSP and the multi-output version of MCSP are also both
known to be NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time
reductions [36], [37].
